d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
Improved tumor control, assessed by reduction in tumor size (RECIST Nano) and clinical symptoms, compared to radiation therapy alone

Enhanced quality of life, evaluated using a standardized assessment grid completed by the owner before, during, and after treatment

Increased longevity, measured by overall survival

Potential for complete response in a subset of patients
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Risks include those associated with anesthesia required for MRI and radiation delivery, as well as risks related to CAR cell injection, such as anaphylactic reactions, transient fever, or cytokines release syndrome.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Dogs with glioma confirmed by biopsy, surgery, or suspected based on MRI findings (as reviewed by a board-certified radiologist or neurologist) are eligible for enrollment.

Both primary tumors and recurrences following surgery may be included.

Patients currently receiving chemotherapy (e.g., temozolomide or lomustine) must discontinue treatment and undergo a washout period of at least two weeks prior to enrollment.

Steroid and anticonvulsant therapies may be continued as prescribed.

All antioxidant supplements, including those marketed as aging or cognitive support medications, must be discontinued. Please consult your primary veterinarian or our study team with any questions or concerns regarding medications or supplements.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
Dogs with a history of prior tumor irradiation

Dogs currently undergoing chemotherapy

Dogs receiving other forms of immunotherapy

These patients are not eligible for enrollment in the study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name:
Dogs will be randomized to receive either CAR-modified cell injection (mod-CAR) or no injection. Radiation therapy may be administered as fractionated radiation (15 × 3 Gy every other day), stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT, 3 × 8 Gy), or Pulsar-adaptive hypofractionated radiation therapy. The radiation modality will be determined during a board review, based on tumor location, size, and histologic type when available.

Baseline assessments will include a physical examination, blood work (CBC and serum chemistry), CT for radiation planning, and MRI if deemed necessary. Radiation will be delivered using an Elekta EVO linear accelerator.

Radiation and mod-CAR therapy will follow one of the three treatment schedules:

  1. Fractionated Radiation Therapy: Dogs will receive 15 radiation fractions every other day (Monday, Wednesday, Friday) under short anesthesia over five weeks. Mod-CAR injections will be administered weekly on Tuesdays for four weeks.
  2. Stereotactic Radiation Therapy (SRT): Dogs will receive three fractions of radiation on alternate days starting Monday of a given week. Mod-CAR will be injected on Tuesday during the radiation week and once again on the Tuesday following the completion of the radiation course.
  3. Pulsar Radiation Therapy Protocol: Dogs will receive Pulsar radiation therapy at a dose of 6–8 Gy every four weeks, for a total of 3 to 5 treatments. Mod-CAR will be administered 48 hours following each radiation session. Patients will undergo monthly re-evaluation, including imaging and multidisciplinary board review. Based on clinical and imaging findings, radiation dose adjustments may be made. Mod-CAR will again be administered 48 hours after any adjusted radiation dose. The maximum cumulative radiation dose will range from 24 to 35 Gy, depending on the fraction size and tumor response.

Weekly blood work (CBC, serum chemistry, and inflammatory profile) will be performed during the radiation period. A first recheck, including blood work, will occur two weeks after completion of radiation.

MRI evaluations will be repeated every three months for one year. Imaging and follow-up costs will be covered by the study.

AE grid criteria form VCO immunotherapy
Adverse effects from anesthesia 
Adverse effects from Radiation VRTOG I and II
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint:
Censoring Guidelines:

Participants will be censored under the following conditions:

  1. Protocol non-compliance: Patients who do not adhere to the prescribed treatment schedule (e.g., missed radiation sessions or investigational drug injections) without a justified reason.
  2. Loss to follow-up: Patients who are unreachable for scheduled evaluations
  3. Unrelated mortality: Deaths clearly attributable to causes unrelated to the disease under investigation (e.g., trauma, cardiac arrest without oncologic link) will be considered as events but not disease-related endpoints.

Study Stopping Criteria:

The study will be halted, either temporarily or permanently, if:

  1. A serious adverse event (SAE) occurs that is determined to be likely related to the intervention (e.g., CAR-modified cell injection or radiation), and is not responsive to standard care management.
  2. A pre-specified threshold of SAEs or treatment-related deaths is met, as defined in the Data and Safety Monitoring Plan (DSMP).
  3. The Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) recommends early termination due to unacceptable toxicity
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_measure: MRI and clinical recheck data will be collected, along with regular phone follow-ups.

d_sv_content.name: CAR neutrophils and Radiation to treat glioma in the dog
d_sv_content.tagline: CAR neutrophils and Radiation  for Dog's glioma
d_sv_content.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that present a significant therapeutic challenge in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by their locally invasive behavior and limited overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds, particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers, are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy can be delivered alone also, through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT), the latter offering greater precision and tissue sparing and short duration treatments. Despite these interventions, prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. The natural disease progression, intact immune system, and comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable in assessing therapeutic efficacy and safety.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy, particularly the use of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered immune cells. CAR technology involves modifying immune cells to express tumor-targeting receptors, enabling them to recognize and destroy cancer cells with heightened specificity. Notably, CAR-engineered neutrophils have demonstrated the ability to traverse the blood-brain barrier—an essential feature for treating intracranial tumors.

A pivotal safety study of CAR neutrophils in dogs was recently conducted at Purdue University, followed by preclinical efficacy testing in murine models of glioma. These genetically modified cells showed potential in targeting brain tumors with minimal off-target toxicity. Building upon these encouraging results, our current research proposes to evaluate the combined therapeutic effect of CAR immunotherapy and radiation therapy in dogs diagnosed with glioma. The rationale is to transform the tumor microenvironment through CAR neutrophils, potentially enhancing the efficacy and outcome of radiation therapy. This synergistic approach may not only improve survival in canine patients but also provide critical translational insights for the treatment of glioblastoma in humans.
